author: Philip K. Dick
card_summary: A very early piece of juvenilia, printed in the Berkeley Daily Gazette's young writers' column on February 17, 1942, when Dick was about thirteen—an artifact of his childhood apprenticeship rather than his mature fiction.
page_summary:
The Jungle People is a brief item Dick published in the Berkeley Daily Gazette on February 17, 1942, in the newspaper's column for young contributors. He was roughly thirteen years old. It is juvenilia in the strict sense—a schoolboy's newspaper piece, preserved here as a two-page scan.

Its interest is biographical rather than literary. It documents that Dick was writing and placing work in print as a child, years before the science-fiction magazine sales of the 1950s. The archive keeps it as evidence of how early his identity as a writer began to form.

Because the surviving text is a short newspaper contribution rather than a developed story, it is best treated as an early trace of the apprenticeship, not as a work bearing his characteristic themes. Its value is as a datable marker at the very start of a long writing life.
